sysd-blocks-112.title: Load balancing: spreading requests across many servers
sysd-blocks-112.text:
A busy website must serve hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of concurrent requests. The cost-effective way to meet that volume is to add more servers. Then something has to decide which server gets which request. That something is a load balancer. Load balancing distributes a set of tasks or incoming network traffic across several computing resources. It sends requests only to those that are online, so the overall work is processed more efficiently.

A load balancer sits in front of the servers and routes each request to one that can fulfil it. It does so in a way that maximizes speed and capacity use, so no single server is overworked. It can improve response time and keeps some nodes from being overloaded while others sit idle. If a server goes down, the balancer redirects traffic to the remaining online servers. When a new server joins the group, requests start flowing to it automatically. That is what makes horizontal scaling work: add servers to the pool and the balancer spreads traffic across all of them.

Load balancing is also widely used for HTTP requests on high-traffic sites, most commonly to provide one Internet service from many servers. Such a group is sometimes known as a server farm. A balancer's main jobs are traffic distribution, availability, SSL termination, keeping a user's session on one server, scaling and keeping track of server health. Which algorithm fits depends on the nature of the tasks, their complexity, the hardware and the error tolerance required, so a compromise must be found for each application.

sysd-blocks-118.title: DNS load balancing: spreading traffic by name lookup
sysd-blocks-118.text:
The simplest load balancer needs no extra machine at all. DNS load balancing configures a domain in the Domain Name System so that client requests to it are spread across a group of servers. Round-robin DNS associates several IP addresses with one domain name and hands them to clients in rotation, with no dedicated software or hardware node.

The limits are real. DNS does not check for server and network outages, so it keeps returning the same IP addresses even when servers are down or unreachable. Returning several records and letting the client choose gives little control, because records are picked randomly and each attracts roughly equal traffic.

DNS delegation does better. A sub-domain such as www is delegated to a zone served by the website's own servers. Each answers with its own address, so a down server simply does not respond. The quickest answer nearly always comes from the closest server, which gives geo-sensitive balancing. A short TTL on the A-record diverts traffic quickly when a server fails.

sysd-blocks-114.title: Load balancing algorithms: rules for picking a server
sysd-blocks-114.text:
How does a balancer choose? The rules it follows are called scheduling algorithms or load-balancing methods, and they decide which back-end server receives each request. The simple ones are random choice, round robin and least connections. Round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin and hash are static algorithms. Least connections and least response time are dynamic ones.

Least connections sends a new request to the server with the fewest current connections to clients, factoring in each server's relative computing capacity, and it can be weighted. Least response time uses a formula that combines the fastest response time and fewest active connections. Least bandwidth picks the server carrying the least traffic in Mbps. Hashing applies a hash function to a key the operator defines, such as the client IP address or the request URL, and routes by the result. Random assignment works quite well, and a random permutation computed in advance avoids per-assignment communication and the need for a distribution master. Power of two choices picks two servers at random and chooses the better of the two.

More sophisticated balancers may also weigh a server's reported load, response times, up or down status from regular checks, active connections, geographic location, capabilities or recently assigned traffic. One source lists least connections among the static methods, so the labels are not universal.

sysd-blocks-120.title: Session persistence: keeping a user on one server
sysd-blocks-120.text:
The next request from a user may land on a server that knows nothing about the last one. Information kept across a session, if stored on one backend server, cannot be found when later requests go to other backends. Session persistence, also called stickiness, is the fix. It sends all requests in one user session to the same backend server so that session data kept there can be found.

Assignment can be based on username, client IP address or random choice. IP-based assignment may be unreliable because of DHCP, network address translation and web proxies. Random assignments must be remembered by the balancer, which costs storage and may be lost if it fails. The client must also keep state, which fails if a browser has disabled cookies.

The significant downside is no automatic recovery. If the backend goes down, its per-session information becomes inaccessible and the sessions that depend on it are lost. Sophisticated balancers use several persistence techniques to avoid the shortcomings of any one.

sysd-blocks-113.title: Static and dynamic load balancing: ignoring load or watching it
sysd-blocks-113.text:
A balancer can follow a plan made in advance, or it can watch what is happening and adapt. A load-balancing algorithm is static when it ignores the current state of the system and dynamic when it takes each node's current load into account.

A static algorithm ignores system state such as processor load. It relies on assumptions made beforehand about arrival times, resource needs and processor speeds. Static algorithms are easy to set up and efficient for fairly regular tasks such as processing HTTP requests from a website. But statistical variance in assignment can still overload some computing units.

Dynamic algorithms use the current load of each node and can move tasks from an overloaded node to an underloaded one for faster processing. They are much more complicated to design, but can improve performance, particularly when execution time varies greatly from one task to another. They need nodes to exchange information, and one that needs too much communication to reach its decisions risks slowing down the overall solution. A dynamic architecture can be more modular, because no specific node has to be dedicated to distributing the work.

Either way, the more is known about the tasks when deciding, the better the optimization. Knowing the exact execution time of every task is an idealized and extremely rare situation.

sysd-blocks-119.title: Client-side load balancing: let the client pick
sysd-blocks-119.text: Sometimes the balancer is the client itself. In client-side random load balancing, the client receives a list of server IPs and picks one at random for each connection. The list is delivered as a DNS list without round-robin, or hardcoded. It relies on all clients generating similar loads and on the law of large numbers to give a reasonably flat distribution across servers. It has been claimed to distribute load better than round-robin DNS, because large DNS servers that remember answers skew round-robin DNS, while random client selection is unaffected. A smart client that detects a down server and connects randomly again can also ride out failures.

sysd-blocks-127.title: Master-worker load balancing: workers ask for tasks
sysd-blocks-127.text: One of the simplest dynamic load balancing algorithms is the master-worker scheme: a master hands out tasks to workers that ask for them. All workers start idle and report to the master, which answers with tasks and tells them to stop asking when none remain. When assignment overhead is low, the work is distributed evenly. But the scheme scales badly to many processors, because of the high amount of communication, and the master is a bottleneck. A task list shared by the processors improves it, though that is slightly harder to implement and still insufficient for very large computing centers.

sysd-blocks-115.title: Round robin load balancing: taking turns
sysd-blocks-115.text: Round robin is load balancing as taking turns. The first request goes to the first server, the next to the second, and so on down to the last, and then the cycle restarts. The services are usually required to be stateless. Weighted round robin lets the administrator give each server a weight, so more powerful servers handle more requests. Sticky round robin improves on it: if a user's first request goes to service A, the following requests go to A as well. When request sizes are homogeneous or unknown, lower-powered units may simply receive fewer requests than larger ones.

sysd-blocks-121.title: Session state storage: where a session can live instead
sysd-blocks-121.text: If session data does not live on one server, the balancer is free to pick any backend. Session state can be kept in a data store, in the client's browser, or in a table spread over many servers. A data store adds load to a system best used for less transient data. In a web browser, the data can live in a time-stamped, encrypted cookie or in rewritten URLs. Client-side storage is generally preferred, though it may not suit large session state, and URL rewriting has major security issues. Spreading named blocks of data over servers by hash is the idea behind {{ref:sysd-scale-139}}.

sysd-blocks-128.title: Work stealing: idle processors take work from busy ones
sysd-blocks-128.text: Work stealing flips the usual question: instead of a balancer pushing tasks out, idle processors pull work in. Each processor is given some tasks, and then idle processors take work from busy or overloaded ones. This overcomes scaling problems when task completion time is unknown. An idle processor asks others at random. If the target can subdivide its task it sends part of it, otherwise it returns an empty task. The method can be particularly effective but is difficult to implement, since communication must not become the processors' main occupation.

sysd-blocks-116.title: Layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing: addresses or content
sysd-blocks-116.text:
A load balancer can look at a request from two very different heights. A layer 4 load balancer routes on transport-level information such as IP addresses and ports. A layer 7 load balancer reads whole requests and routes on their content.

A layer 4 balancer works at the transport layer. It routes on network information such as IP addresses and TCP and UDP ports, so it cannot perform content-based routing. These balancers are often dedicated hardware devices that can operate at high speed.

A layer 7 balancer works at the application layer, reads requests in their entirety and performs content-based routing. Load can then be managed from a full understanding of the traffic. It comes in variations. Host-based routing uses the requested hostname, path-based routing uses the entire URL, and content-based routing inspects the message, for example the value of a parameter. Routing by URL needs plain HTTP, or HTTPS that is terminated (decrypted) at the balancer. Platform-specific routing can send requests from different device types, such as mobiles and desktops, to specialized backend systems.

sysd-blocks-117.title: Hardware, software and cloud load balancers
sysd-blocks-117.text: A load balancer can be a box in a rack, a program on an ordinary machine or a managed service in the cloud. A hardware balancer is physical on-premises equipment that handles a large volume of traffic. It often costs a lot, is fairly inflexible and runs proprietary firmware that needs patches. Software balancers are usually easier to deploy, cost-effective and flexible, at the cost of more set-up work. Cloud balancers such as AWS Elastic Load Balancer are built into the provider's infrastructure.

sysd-blocks-126.title: Global server load balancing: balancing across the world
sysd-blocks-126.text: When a service's users are spread across the world, its balancing can be spread too. Global server load balancing distributes traffic across multiple geographical locations to improve performance at a global scale. Cross-zone load balancing distributes incoming traffic across geographic or network zones, which increases the system's resilience and its capacity for large volumes of requests. DNS-based delegation gives geo-sensitive balancing, since the quickest DNS response is nearly always from the network's closest server. For content delivery, server-load balancing uses service-based (global load balancing) or hardware-based techniques, such as layer 4-7 switches, to share traffic among several servers or web caches.

sysd-blocks-122.title: Health checks: noticing which servers are down
sysd-blocks-122.text: A balancer is only as useful as its picture of which servers are alive. A health check lets the load balancer tell whether a server is down or performing poorly so it can remove that server from the pool. The balancer polls servers for application-layer health and removes failed servers. It monitors components continually, for example web servers by fetching known pages. When one becomes unresponsive, the balancer stops sending it traffic, and it resumes when the server is back online. This continuous evaluation directs requests only to instances that are fully operational, which maintains performance and keeps service uninterrupted.

sysd-blocks-123.title: Load balancer failover: staying up when a server fails
sysd-blocks-123.text:
When a server dies, the balancer is the one that notices. Load balancing is often used to keep service going after the failure of one or more components. The balancer is informed when a component fails, stops sending it traffic, and reroutes traffic to it when it returns. For this to work there must be at least one component in excess of the service's capacity, an arrangement called N+1. That is much cheaper and more flexible than pairing every live component with a standby that takes over on failure.

The catch is that the balancer itself can become the one part whose failure stops everything. To avoid that, a second or N load balancers can run in cluster mode, and if the active one fails, a passive one takes over. Balancers are usually implemented in high-availability pairs, which may also replicate session persistence data if the application needs it. Some balancers do something special when all backend servers are unavailable, such as forwarding to a spare balancer or displaying a message about the outage.

sysd-blocks-124.title: TLS termination: decrypting at the balancer
sysd-blocks-124.text: TLS encryption can become a major part of a web server's CPU demand. A load balancer can terminate TLS connections itself: it decrypts the traffic and passes plain HTTP requests to the backend servers. It can then also balance or switch content based on data inside the HTTPS request. The downside is that all TLS processing is concentrated on one device, which can become a new bottleneck. Adding a few web servers may be cheaper than upgrading it. The balancer also needs the TLS certificate and private key, which widens access to unencrypted data and makes it a more valuable attack target.

sysd-blocks-125.title: Load balancer features: beyond handing out requests
sysd-blocks-125.text:
Distributing requests is only the beginning of what balancers do. The fundamental feature is spreading incoming requests over the backend servers in the cluster according to a scheduling algorithm. Most other features are vendor specific.

Some features manage load. Asymmetric load assigns a manual ratio so some backends get a bigger share, a simple way to reflect capacity differences. Priority activation brings standby servers online when too few servers remain or load is too high. Connection multiplexing consolidates multiple HTTP requests from multiple clients into a single TCP socket to the backends. TCP buffering spoon-feeds responses to slow clients so web server threads are freed sooner. HTTP compression cuts transferred data and helps more for larger responses and distant clients. It adds CPU demand on the balancer, though, and could be done by the web servers instead. An application-layer balancer may also cache static content to answer some requests without contacting the servers.

Others protect and observe. Balancers can mitigate SYN flood attacks with SYN cookies and delayed binding, where backends do not see the client until it completes its TCP handshake. HTTP security features include hiding error pages, removing server identification headers and encrypting cookies so end users cannot manipulate them. Logging request and response metadata gives an audit trail or analytics data, and request tracing gives each request a unique id for logging and troubleshooting.

openers.load-balancing: Once one server cannot carry the traffic, you add more servers, and then something has to decide who gets each request. Load balancing distributes incoming network traffic across several computing resources, sending requests only to those that are online. This chapter looks at where that decision can be made, in the DNS, in the client or in a dedicated balancer, and at the rules for making it, from taking turns to picking the least busy server. It also covers keeping a user's session together, whether a balancer reads addresses or whole requests, and what happens when a server, or the balancer itself, fails.

reviews.load-balancing: Every balancer answers one question, which server gets this request, and the answers differ in where they run and what they know. Round robin is static, ignoring the system's state, while dynamic methods such as least connections and master-worker take each node's current load into account. Layer 4 balancers route on addresses and ports, layer 7 balancers on content, and either can be hardware, software or a cloud service. Health checks, spare capacity and balancers in pairs keep a failure from taking the service down. Session state kept in a shared store or in the client frees the balancer to send a user to any server.
